items.title: Inside Saudi Arabia, Houthi attacks test kingdom's image of security
items.summary: Despite the strikes, markets and restaurants in Riyadh remain busy as residents express trust in the government to protect them.
items.body:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Houthis said they were responsible for an attack on an oil facility south of Riyadh on 3 October, one of a growing number

ByNawal Al-Maghafi

Senior international investigations correspondent, Reporting fromRiyadh

Ten days after fleeing his home in Yemen's capital, Sanaa, Abu Khalil is selling socks on the streets of Riyadh.

"I walked out of Sanaa, I crossed the front line," he says, adding that he "hitched a ride into Saudi Arabia".

Families in Yemen are "struggling to provide for [their] children", he says, as he tries to earn enough to send some money home.

He asks us not to use his full name because his wife and four children are still in Sanaa, and he is frightened of what might happen to them if he is identified speaking out against the Houthis. "I ran away from the Houthis but I couldn't bring my family with me. May God protect them," he says.

Backed by Iran, the armed group has controlled much of northern Yemen since a civil war erupted more than a decade ago. It is fighting the internationally recognised government, which is supported by neighbouring Saudi Arabia.

And Saudi cities, such as Riyadh, are now coming under regular drone and missile attacks from the very group Abu Khalil fled.

An informal ceasefire in Yemen unravelled in July, and since the fighting escalated, the Houthis have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia. They have said they were retaliating against deadly Saudi air strikes in Yemen and what they say is a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled territory.

One Houthi strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured more than 300 - the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in years.

Image source, Saudi Ministry of Media/Reuters

Image caption,

Surveillance footage shows the moment of the attack at King Khalid International Airport on 10 October

Having been granted rare permission to report from Riyadh, we spoke to locals, including Majid, a 25-year-old engineer who works for the Saudi state oil company Aramco. He was passing through the airport that day, rushing for a flight to Jeddah for a religious pilgrimage.

He says he was watching a mother push her children in a pushchair when the terminal was hit.

He remembers seeing a man covered in blood. "I went to him in shock, asking him, 'Are you OK?'" He says he saw injured and unconscious passengers being taken to the airport's first aid clinic.

"Some of them, I still don't know whether they were alive or not."

The experience left him shaken. "The threat is real," he tells me. "But I will not let the Houthis make me feel unsafe in my own country."

The airport attack was far from an isolated incident. BBC analysis of data from the US-based Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (Acled), a non-profit organisation, which collects data on political violence and protests around the world, identified 274 attacks on Saudi Arabia in almost five months between 1 July and 25 November.

According to Acled, most of these were intercepted, but at least 41 were not and in some cases debris from the interception also caused damage.

Drones featured in almost two-thirds of the attacks, while ballistic missiles were used in more than half, according to the data.

In the previous five months, Acled recorded just one Houthi attack on the country.

Backed by Iran, the Houthis have developed an increasingly sophisticated arsenal, dramatically extending their ability to repeatedly strike deep in Saudi territory.

For years, Houthi attacks were largely concentrated near the Yemeni border, with Riyadh targeted far less frequently. But since the collapse of the unofficial ceasefire, the Saudi capital, more than 700km (430 miles) away from the Yemeni border, is now coming under regular attack.

As well as the airport, oil installations and prominent buildings in the capital have been in danger.

Saudi Arabia has spent billions transforming its cities, attracting international investment and presenting itself to the world as a safe place to live, work and visit - the attacks have put this promise to the test.

Two prominent skyscrapers have been hit in Riyadh's financial district this month.

Image source, Saudi Press Agency/Reuters

Image caption,

Saudi Arabia's tallest skyscraper, the PIF tower, was struck on 19 November

Eleven people were injured in a strike on the Public Investment Fund (PIF) Tower, which is the tallest in Saudi Arabia and is the headquarters of the country's sovereign wealth fund. The other was the Aramco building, home to the state oil company.

As we drove past the Aramco tower, the damage was a clear reminder of the threat facing the kingdom.

But within days, the building's exterior had been completely repaired, any visible sign of the attack erased. It was perhaps a reflection of Saudi Arabia's determination to project an image of stability and business as usual, even as the attacks continue.

The government has condemned "terrorist attacks targeting civilian and economic facilities" and said it would "take all necessary measures" to defend itself.

Even so, flights to the capital have been severely disrupted by the strikes, which have also targeted other locations, such as Medina and the airport in the eastern city of Dammam.

Many passengers travelling to Riyadh are being routed through different airports and making the final leg of the journey on land.

The flight we took to Dammam was almost empty. Riyadh's streets tell a different story, though.

Image source, BBC/Liam Weir

Image caption,

Stallholders in Riyadh's markets are trading as normal

Restaurants are bustling, families browse at shopping centres and people go about their evenings seemingly undeterred by the threat overhead.

But getting people to speak openly about the conflict is difficult in a country where strict censorship laws and restrictions on freedom of expression make many wary of talking to the media.

Many of those who did speak to us expressed confidence in their country's ability to protect them. At a busy market, Badr says the airport attack was worrying, but life has quickly returned to normal. "I sleep comfortably," he says, praising the country's security forces.

Another man, Rashid, gestures towards the stalls around us: "The market is booming. People are buying and selling, going about their business. Everything is good."

But the normality he describes is periodically disturbed by a sudden buzz on the phone with an alert warning of an incoming attack. Then come the loud booms of air defences intercepting missiles and drones overhead.

We experienced one at 04:00 one morning, and the knowledge that not every attack is being intercepted can leave people afraid.

Image source, BBC/Liam Weir

Image caption,

Alex Malouf says the attacks and alerts can be hard for children to deal with

British expatriate Alex Malouf, who has lived in Saudi Arabia on and off since 2006, says he worries about the psychological impact on his 11-year-old daughter, who has experienced security alerts while at school.

"There have been times when my daughter has said, 'Daddy, I'm scared.' It has been something which I think has shaken our reality."

Despite the attacks, Abu Khalil says he feels much safer in Saudi Arabia than at home in Yemen where fighting has intensified.

The Houthis' renewed offensive in western Yemen has seen the group capture territory along the Red Sea coast and threaten strategic routes towards the southern city of Aden, the government's temporary base.

Image source, EPA/Shutterstock

Image caption,

The wreckage of a shoe factory following a Saudi-led strike on Sanaa on 17 November

The fighting has also intensified around Taiz, a government-controlled city that has endured years of siege and conflict.

Road closures resulting from the latest Houthi siege there have severely restricted deliveries of essential supplies, leaving more than 800,000 people cut off from humanitarian assistance, according to the UN children's agency Unicef. Food and fuel that can be found have shot up in price.

More than 360,000 people have been forced from their homes in Yemen since August, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). And the UN Human Rights Office has verified 323 civilian casualties since then, including 76 killed, with children accounting for half of the dead.

A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has responded to the Houthi advances and attacks on the kingdom with intensified air strikes, adding to the dangers faced by civilians. One strike in Sanaa earlier this month killed 44 people, according to Houthi authorities. Saudi Arabia says these operations were to protect the Yemeni population and global trade from the Houthis.

Saudi-led bombing campaigns during the earlier years of the war killed thousands of civilians and devastated homes, hospitals and schools.

The Houthis have also inflicted enormous suffering on civilians through shelling, missile and ground attacks on government-held territory, as well as repression in areas under their control.

Abu Khalil hopes that he will soon be able to bring his wife and children over to Saudi Arabia, away from the dangers in Sanaa, and says he "will not go back until the Houthis are gone".

Additional reporting by Jasmin Dyer and Ahmed Nour

items.title: Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson launches last-ditch High Court appeal
items.summary: Erin Patterson is serving life in prison for poisoning her relatives with a toxic mushroom lunch in 2023.
items.body:
Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

Patterson was last year found guilty of murdering three relatives

BySimon Atkinson

Australia's mushroom killer Erin Patterson has launched a final legal bid to overturn her murder convictions and avoid dying in jail.

Erin Patterson, 52, was last year found guilty of murdering three relatives and attempting to kill another when she served them a toxic mushroom-laced meal in 2023.

Last month, in Victoria's Court of Appeal three judges dismissed an appeal against her convictions and threw out the possibility she could be released on parole – saying her crimes were "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and had to be "denounced in the strongest terms".

She has now made a last-ditch application to the High Court to look at her case.

Patterson had 28 days to file an application for special leave to appeal to the High Court, a deadline which expired on Friday.

She wants the country's top judges to examine both her conviction and sentence - but the court does not have to agree to look at the case. It only hears appeals in about 10% of cases.

After a high-profile trial last year, a jury found Patterson guilty of murdering her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, by serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms which she had tracked down, foraged and prepared.

Patterson was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, who also ate the toxic lunch at Patterson's home in rural Victoria.

He survived after spending weeks in hospital and has ongoing health issues due to the poisoning.

Simon Patterson, the host's estranged husband, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.

Patterson was sentenced last September, with the trial judge allowing a non-parole period of 33 years due to the "harsh prison conditions" she would likely face. This glimmer of hope of freedom was thrown out by the appeal judges, who ruled she should never be released.

She had argued her conviction was unsafe on seven grounds - including a hotel booking mix up which saw the jury stay in the same place as the prosecution, a key police witness and the media.

Her lawyers said this was "catastrophic" and undermined the integrity of her trial, but the appeal court judges dismissed all the grounds for appeal.

translation.body:
图片来源，路透社

图片说明，

帕特森去年被判谋杀三名亲属罪名成立

作者：西蒙·阿特金森

澳大利亚蘑菇杀手艾琳·帕特森已发起最后的法律努力，试图推翻其谋杀罪名并避免死于狱中。

52岁的艾琳·帕特森去年被判罪名成立，罪名是2023年她在一顿掺有毒蘑菇的餐食中谋杀三名亲属并企图杀害另一人。

上个月，在维多利亚州上诉法院，三名法官驳回了对她定罪的上诉，并排除了她获得假释的可能性——称她的罪行“极其冷酷且蓄意”，必须“以最强烈的措辞予以谴责”。

她现已向高等法院提出最后申请，要求审理她的案件。

帕特森有28天时间提交向高等法院申请上诉特别许可，该截止日期已于周五到期。

她希望该国最高法官同时审查她的定罪和量刑——但法院不必同意审理此案。法院只审理约10%的上诉案件。

在去年一场备受关注的审判后，陪审团裁定帕特森罪名成立，认定她通过向公婆唐和盖尔·帕特森以及盖尔的妹妹希瑟·威尔金森分别提供含有毒鹅膏菌的惠灵顿牛排而谋杀他们，这些蘑菇是她追踪、采集并烹制的。

帕特森还被判企图谋杀希瑟的丈夫伊恩·威尔金森罪名成立，伊恩是当地牧师，他也在帕特森位于维多利亚州乡村的家中食用了那顿有毒午餐。

他在住院数周后幸存，但因中毒仍有持续的健康问题。

女主人的分居丈夫西蒙·帕特森本应参加那顿午餐，但在最后一刻取消，部分原因是他相信妻子多年来多次试图毒害他。

帕特森于去年9月被判刑，主审法官考虑到她可能面临的“严酷监狱条件”，允许33年的非假释期。这一线自由的希望被上诉法官驳回，他们裁定她永远不应获释。

她曾以七项理由主张其定罪不安全——包括一次酒店预订混乱，导致陪审团与控方、一名关键警方证人和媒体住在同一地点。

她的律师称这是“灾难性的”，损害了审判的公正性，但上诉法院法官驳回了所有上诉理由。

items.title: Venezuela to scrap law that bars opposition from public office
items.summary: The legislation has been criticised for enabling political persecution since it was introduced two years ago.
items.body:
Image source, EPA

Image caption,

Jorge Rodríguez said no politician had been subjected to the law's provisions

ByChris Graham

Venezuela will repeal a law that bars opposition figures from assuming public office, the speaker of the National Assembly Jorge Rodríguez has said.

The legislation, which was introduced two years ago, has been criticised for enabling political persecution, but Rodríguez said no politician had been subjected to its provisions.

The older brother of Venezuela's interim president Delcy Rodríguez said he expected the reforms to be approved next week.

Delcy Rodríguez's interim government has been negotiating with opposition parties since taking over at the start of the year, when former President Nicolás Maduro was seized by the United States.

The legislation, known as the Simón Bolívar Law, was passed shortly after the election in July 2024 in which then-incumbent Maduro was declared the winner amid widespread allegations of fraud.

Under the legislation, individuals who requested or supported foreign sanctions against Venezuela were permanently banned from political office and had their assets confiscated.

"Legislative processes are dynamic processes. That law responded to a very specific moment in a particular situation that Venezuela was going through," Jorge Rodríguez said.

During subsequent talks, which began in August, the interim government and parts of the opposition agreed to review several other laws as part of a "route map towards democracy", according to an opposition statement.

Delcy Rodríguez has promised that the South American country will hold free and fair elections, without setting a date.

Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado is widely expected to run for office in the event of an election despite being excluded from transition talks.

Machado returned to the country in October after more than 10 months in exile.

In the 2024 election, Machado's ally Edmundo González ran in her place after she was barred from running for office by Maduro's government.

The electoral authority, which was closely aligned with the government, declared Maduro the winner without making detailed voting tallies public.

The opposition argued that González won the election, not Maduro, uploading copies of the voting tallies as evidence.

作者：克里斯·格雷厄姆

委内瑞拉国民议会议长豪尔赫·罗德里格斯表示，委内瑞拉将废除一项禁止反对派人士担任公职的法律。

这项立法于两年前推出，因助长政治迫害而受到批评，但罗德里格斯表示，没有政治家受到其条款的约束。

自今年年初前总统尼古拉斯·马杜罗被美国抓获、德尔西·罗德里格斯的临时政府接管以来，该政府一直在与反对党进行谈判。

New Zealand’s ruling coalition falls just short of majority in final election count

If Prime Minister Christopher Luxon cannot reach a deal to form a ruling coalition, New Zealand will have to hold fresh elections.

People enter a voting place at St Anne’s Anglican Church on the day of the general election in Wellington, New Zealand, Nov 7, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Hollie Adams)

WELLINGTON: New Zealand’s ruling centre-right coalition has narrowly missed winning a parliamentary majority, final election results showed on Friday (Nov 27), leaving Prime Minister Christopher Luxon needing the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power.

If Luxon cannot reach either a coalition or confidence-and-supply deal, and any negotiations between other parties fail to produce a majority government, New Zealand will have to hold fresh elections.

Electoral Commission results showed the coalition with 65 seats, one seat short of a majority in the 130-seat parliament.

"New Zealanders need a government that is stable, that works together and will last for the full term," Luxon told a news conference.

"Kiwis won’t thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart or for sending them back to the polls."

OPPORTUNITY TO NEGOTIATE WITH NATIONAL

Luxon’s centre-right National Party secured 40 seats in the Nov 7 election, and its junior coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First won 13 seats and 12 seats, respectively.

Labour, the largest opposition party, won 36 seats.

New entrant to parliament Opportunity won seven seats, and its leader Qiulae Wong said on Friday she would negotiate with National as the party with the largest number of seats.

"I don't think anybody can rule anything out at this stage because we haven't had any discussions," Wong told a press conference, adding all options were on the table including being on the crossbenches.

New Zealand poised for weeks of political wrangling after knife-edge poll

New Zealand’s centrist kingmaker says populism failing voters worldwide

"We are going to do everything we can to make sure that there is a stable government," she said.

Opportunity's platform includes stronger climate commitments, a ban on bottom-trawling fishing, tighter competition rules and a more interventionist approach to public investment, policies that cut against parts of the coalition's agenda.

ACT Party leader David Seymour said government formation could happen "quite rapidly" if the parties involved worked together to come to an agreement.

"The government can be formed if the coalition is prepared to work with Opportunity at some level," he said in an interview with 1News.

The results show a centre-left coalition of Labour, the Green Party and Te Pati Maori would not be able to form a government, even with the support of Opportunity.

However, if NZ First were to strike a deal with the centre-left parties — as it did with Labour after the 2017 election — they could form a coalition government.

The New Zealand dollar, which hit a 17-year low against the US dollar this week, strengthened slightly after the announcement of the election results.

Earlier this month, preliminary results from the Electoral Commission had shown the ruling coalition with a majority of two seats. The final tally includes special votes, which include those from people voting overseas or outside their electorate, and typically skew left.

The Electoral Commission said there were 2,931,604 votes cast, of which 484,865 were special votes.

WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump said on Thursday (Nov 26) that he had seen sufficient information that Nvidia's Jensen Huang was not a security threat, while touting his administration's intervention to save the scandal-plagued CEO's job as "a great thing" for the world.

"I think he's absolutely fine," Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago estate.

Asked by AFP how he could be sure when the Justice Department would not confirm it had conducted a thorough investigation into Huang, Trump said his belief was based on "information I have, which is a lot of information".

items.title: Met Police ruined my life, says Kenyan man wrongly convicted over attack on UK couple
items.summary: Evidence from a British police officer helped convict Ali Kololo over a 2011 attack in the Kenyan resort of Lamu.
items.body:
Figure caption,

Watch: Man wrongly sentenced to death says Met Police ruined his life

ByJean Mackenzie

Reporting fromLamu

A Kenyan woodcutter who was wrongly sentenced to death over an attack on a British couple has told the BBC that actions by London's Metropolitan Police involved in the case destroyed his life.

Somali gunmen broke into David and Judith Tebbutt's beach bungalow on the Kenyan coast in 2011. They shot David dead and abducted Judith, holding her captive in Somalia for six months.

Met detectives flew to Kenya to assist the investigation. Their evidence helped convict Ali Kololo, who spent more than a decade in prison before his conviction was overturned.

Kololo is suing the Met, claiming a senior officer, former Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, gave misleading evidence at his trial and acted unlawfully to secure his conviction.

In his first media interview, he told the BBC about his 15-year ordeal and his fight for compensation, which the Met is challenging in court.

We meet on Lamu, a small island off Kenya's northern coast, once a thriving Swahili port. People and goods are still carted through its narrow stone streets by donkey rather than car.

It was here, in 2013, that Kololo was sentenced to death.

Standing at the jetty, where police once brought him ashore in handcuffs, he relishes being free. But he is struggling to rebuild his life.

"Everything was taken from me. I'm starting from zero. I don't think I'll ever go back to who I was before," he says.

Image source, Judith Tebbutt

Image caption,

David and Judith Tebbutt were on a dream holiday to Kenya when they were attacked

Before his arrest, Kololo lived with his wife and their three young children. He had once worked as a groundskeeper at the resort where the Tebbutts were staying, but by 2011 he earned his living felling trees in a local forest and selling the wood.

"My life was very good," he says. "I was fending for myself, taking good care of my family."

Within 24 hours of the attack, Kenyan police had arrested him.

"I was beaten with clubs and thrown into a car," he says. "They beat me for days, burning me with cigarettes, forcing me to confess to things. They subjected me to torture like no other."

Kololo could not read or write. He says police made him put his thumbprint on a statement claiming he had led the attackers to the Tebbutts.

"I didn't understand anything," he says, calling the statement "a mountain of lies". "I signed it without knowing what it was because of the state they had put me in".

The Kenyan police told us it "at all times strives to work within the law". Kololo is not suing them.

Image caption,

Ali Kololo says he lost contact with his children while he was in prison

Within days of the attack, a team of Met officers, led by then Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, arrived to support the Kenyan investigation. The UK government had instructed the officers not to accept information from the Kenyan authorities that had been obtained by interrogating detainees.

But Hibberd requested Kololo's statement and later relied on it when giving evidence for the prosecution at his trial.

In court, Hibberd also presented evidence linking Kololo to the attack. He told the Kenyan court Kololo had been wearing a type of shoe that matched footwear marks found in the sand at the resort.

The officer who had arrested Kololo said he was barefoot when he was handed to police. Hibberd did not disclose that the Met's own forensic examination could not establish whether the shoe in question had made the marks.

At the trial, Kololo did not initially have a lawyer. He had to cross-examine all the prosecution witnesses himself, including Hibberd, through an interpreter who spoke Swahili, which was not Kololo's first language.

"I believe I was framed because I am a poor man and I did not have the strength or means to fight for myself," Kololo says.

Kololo was convicted of kidnap and robbery with violence - the only person ever convicted in connection with the attack. He spent three years on death row before his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.

He recalls seeing his prison file. In the space for the expiry date, someone had written "death".

Years later, the UK's Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) established that Hibberd had omitted significant forensic evidence at the trial. It found that he would have had a case to answer for gross misconduct, but he could not face disciplinary proceedings because he had retired from the force. Image caption,

Neil Hibberd retired from the police in 2017

In April 2023, Kenya's High Court quashed Kololo's conviction, because of doubts over the prosecution's evidence. This followed years of work by the legal charity Reprieve and a Kenyan lawyer, Alfred Olaba, who represented him for free.

They were supported by Judith Tebbutt, who believed Kololo was innocent. In an interview with the BBC in 2022, she said he had been scapegoated by Scotland Yard.

"He was not there on the night. He was not part of the group that held me. They've put this man in prison without any real evidence."

More than three years after his release, Kololo says he is still living with the effects of his torture and decade in prison. As we walk the narrow streets of Lamu's old town, his thin frame moves stiffly. He is on edge. "My mind is not good," he says. "I have not recovered."

He remembers being kept in a filthy, bedbug-ridden cell with up to eight other inmates, which he thought he would never leave. Twice he contracted tuberculosis and nearly died.

Kololo is now too frail to do the woodcutting he once relied on to make a living. He tries to grow enough to eat on the land around his home, but erratic rain makes it difficult.

"I have nothing. On the days I get food, I eat, and on the days I don't, I endure."

He lives alone in a mud hut. His wife divorced him after he went to prison, and their children went to live with his mother. They dropped out of school because the family could not pay the fees. Kololo says they were not allowed to visit him in prison. When he was released, they barely remembered him, especially his youngest.

"They were too young. Only now are they starting to regain the memory that 'this is our father who disappeared'," he says. "If it weren't for my mother, my children might have died."

For much of our time together, Kololo is remarkably upbeat. He trusts that his lawyers and God will deliver him justice. But when we talk about the Met, his demeanour shifts.

"I am extremely angry with the police," he says. "I'm also angry with the Kenyan Police. They collaborated to incriminate me. What [Hibberd] said destroyed my entire life and my children's lives."

The Met has not apologised to Kololo or admitted wrongdoing. The force is contesting his compensation claim, which his lawyers say could take years to resolve.

"These people falsely accused me. Do I not deserve something?" he asks.

The Met told the BBC that neither they nor Hibberd wanted to comment on Kololo's claim, but it said: "Our thoughts are with Mr Kololo, Mrs Tebbutt, her family and all those who have been affected by this terrible crime. The Metropolitan Police remains committed to supporting the Kenyan authorities in any way that may be possible, in order to get justice for Mrs Tebbutt and her late husband."

Preetha Gopalan, Reprieve's head of UK litigation, describes the Met's behaviour in Kololo's case as "egregious".

"They've spent 10 years trying to evade accountability in every way possible, now dragging him through the courts," she says. "It's possible for them to do the right thing, but they are unwilling, and so this ordeal continues to haunt Kololo and his family."

"Even if I get a billion shillings, I will never be the same," Kololo says. "But if I get the justice I deserve, I can help my children and take care of myself when I am an old man."

translation.title: 肯尼亚男子因袭击英国夫妇被错误定罪，称伦敦警察厅毁了我的人生
translation.summary: 一名英国警察提供的证据帮助判定阿里·科洛洛（Ali Kololo）在 2011 年肯尼亚拉穆度假地袭击案中有罪。
translation.label: 机器翻译
translation.summary_source: Evidence from a British police officer helped convict Ali Kololo over a 2011 attack in the Kenyan resort of Lamu.
translation.body:
图片说明，

观看：被错误判处死刑的男子称伦敦警察厅毁了他的人生

作者：Jean Mackenzie

发自拉穆

一名因一起针对英国夫妇的袭击案而被错误判处死刑的肯尼亚伐木工告诉BBC，伦敦大都会警察局在此案中的行为毁了他的人生。

2011年，索马里枪手闯入David和Judith Tebbutt位于肯尼亚海岸的海滩平房。他们开枪打死了David，并绑架了Judith，将她囚禁在索马里长达六个月。

大都会警察局的侦探飞往肯尼亚协助调查。他们的证据帮助定罪了Ali Kololo，后者在狱中度过了十多年，直到其定罪被推翻。

Kololo正在起诉大都会警察局，声称一名高级警官、前侦缉警司Neil Hibberd在其审判中提供了误导性证据，并以非法手段确保其被定罪。

在首次接受媒体采访时，他向BBC讲述了自己15年的磨难以及为争取赔偿而进行的斗争，大都会警察局正在法庭上对此提出异议。

我们在他乡拉穆见面，这是肯尼亚北部海岸外的一座小岛，曾是繁荣的斯瓦希里港口。人们和货物仍然靠驴而不是汽车穿过狭窄的石板街道。

正是在这里，2013年，Kololo被判处死刑。

站在码头边——警察曾戴着手铐将他带上岸的地方——他享受着自由。但他正艰难地重建自己的生活。

“我的一切都被夺走了。我从零开始。我觉得我永远也回不到从前的自己了，”他说。

图片来源，Judith Tebbutt

图片说明，

David和Judith Tebbutt当时正在肯尼亚度梦想假期，却遭到了袭击

被捕前，Kololo与妻子和三个年幼的孩子住在一起。他曾一度在Tebbutt夫妇下榻的度假村做场地管理员，但到2011年，他靠在当地森林里伐木卖木材为生。

“我的生活非常好，”他说。“我自食其力，好好照顾家人。”

袭击发生后24小时内，肯尼亚警方就逮捕了他。

“我被棍棒殴打，然后被扔进一辆车里，”他说。“他们打了我好几天，用香烟烫我，逼我承认一些事情。他们对我施加了前所未有的酷刑。”

Kololo不识字。他说，警方强迫他在一份声明上按下拇指印，声明称是他把袭击者带到了Tebbutt夫妇那里。

“我什么都不明白，”他说，称这份声明是“一座谎言之山”。“我在不知道那是什么的情况下签了字，因为他们把我置于那种境地”。

肯尼亚警方告诉我们，他们“始终努力在法律范围内行事”。Kololo没有起诉他们。

图片说明，

Ali Kololo说他在狱中与孩子们失去了联系

袭击发生后的几天内，一支由时任侦缉警司Neil Hibberd领导的大都会警察局警官团队抵达，以支持肯尼亚的调查。英国政府曾指示这些警官不要接受肯尼亚当局通过审讯被拘留者获得的信息。

但Hibberd索要了Kololo的声明，后来在审判中为控方作证时又依据了这份声明。

在法庭上，Hibberd还出示了将Kololo与袭击联系起来的证据。他告诉肯尼亚法庭，Kololo当时穿的鞋子与度假村沙滩上发现的鞋印相符。

逮捕Kololo的警官说，他被交给警方时是赤脚的。Hibberd没有披露，大都会警察局自己的法医鉴定无法确定涉案鞋子是否留下了那些印记。

在审判中，Kololo最初没有律师。他不得不亲自盘问所有控方证人，包括Hibberd，而且是通过一名说斯瓦希里语的翻译——斯瓦希里语并非Kololo的母语。

“我相信我是被陷害的，因为我是个穷人，我没有力量或手段为自己抗争，”Kololo说。

Kololo被判犯有绑架和暴力抢劫罪——他是此案中唯一被定罪的人。他在死囚牢房中度过了三年，之后刑期被减为终身监禁。

他回忆起看到自己的监狱档案。在到期日期一栏，有人写了“死亡”。

“我彻底心碎了。我相信我随时可能被处决，我将再也见不到我的家人、我的孩子。”

多年后，英国警察行为独立办公室（IOPC）认定，Hibberd在审判中遗漏了重要的法医证据。该机构认为，他本应因严重不当行为而面临问责，但由于他已从警队退休，无法面临纪律处分程序。当时，他的律师表示，Hibberd完全不同意报告的结论。

图片来源，shutterstock

图片说明，

Neil Hibberd于2017年从警队退休

2023年4月，肯尼亚高等法院因对控方证据存疑而撤销了对Kololo的定罪。此前，法律慈善机构Reprieve和肯尼亚律师Alfred Olaba经过多年努力，后者免费为他代理。

他们得到了Judith Tebbutt的支持，她相信Kololo是无辜的。在2022年接受BBC采访时，她说他被伦敦警察厅当成了替罪羊。

“那天晚上他不在那里。他不是扣押我的那伙人中的一员。他们在没有任何真正证据的情况下把这个人关进了监狱。”

获释三年多后，Kololo说，他仍然承受着酷刑和十年监禁带来的影响。当我们走在拉穆老城狭窄的街道上时，他瘦削的身躯僵硬地移动着。他紧张不安。“我的精神状态不好，”他说。“我还没有恢复。”

他记得自己被关在一间肮脏、满是臭虫的牢房里，最多与另外八名囚犯关在一起，他以为自己永远也出不去了。他两次感染肺结核，险些丧命。

Kololo现在身体太虚弱，无法再做他曾经赖以为生的伐木工作。他试图在家周围的土地上种出足够的食物，但雨水不稳定使这变得困难。

“我一无所有。有食物的日子我就吃，没有的日子我就忍着。”

他独自住在一间泥屋里。他入狱后妻子与他离婚，孩子们去和祖母住。由于家里付不起学费，他们辍学了。Kololo说，他们不被允许来监狱探望他。他获释时，他们几乎不记得他了，尤其是最小的孩子。

“他们太小了。直到现在他们才开始恢复记忆，知道‘这是那个消失了的父亲’，”他说。“如果不是我母亲，我的孩子们可能已经死了。”

在我们相处的大部分时间里，Kololo非常乐观。他相信他的律师和上帝会为他伸张正义。但当我们谈到伦敦警察厅时，他的神态变了。

“我对警察极其愤怒，”他说。“我也对肯尼亚警方愤怒。他们勾结起来陷害我。[Hibberd]说的话毁了我的一生和我孩子们的生活。”

伦敦警察厅没有向Kololo道歉，也没有承认不当行为。该警局正在对他的赔偿要求提出异议，他的律师说，这可能要花数年时间才能解决。

“这些人诬告了我。难道我不该得到些什么吗？”他问道。

伦敦警察厅告诉BBC，他们和Hibberd都不想就Kololo的索赔发表评论，但表示：“我们与Kololo先生、Tebbutt夫人、她的家人以及所有受这起可怕罪行影响的人同在。大都会警察局仍然致力于以任何可能的方式支持肯尼亚当局，为Tebbutt夫人及其已故丈夫伸张正义。”

Reprieve英国诉讼负责人Preetha Gopalan将伦敦警察厅在Kololo案中的行为描述为“极其恶劣”。

“他们十年来一直想方设法逃避问责，现在又把他拖上法庭，”她说。“他们本可以做出正确的事，但他们不愿意，因此这场磨难继续困扰着Kololo和他的家人。”

“即使我得到十亿先令，我也永远不会和以前一样了，”Kololo说。“但如果我得到我应得的正义，我就能帮助我的孩子，并在年老时照顾自己。”

items.title: Sheikh Hasina's planned return puts Bangladesh on edge - and India in a bind
items.summary: The ousted prime minister's December homecoming plan deepens Dhaka-Delhi tensions and risks fresh unrest.
items.body:
Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty Images

Image caption,

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi with Sheikh Hasina in Delhi in 2024 - Hasina was a close ally of India during her years in power

By

Soutik Biswas

India correspondent

Sheikh Hasina has repeatedly vowed to return to Bangladesh.

Now the ousted prime minister has put a date on her homecoming - 16 December - and even outlined how she intends to make the journey.

The government in Dhaka, which had previously dismissed the prospect, is taking her latest declaration more seriously.

Hasina, 79, who fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule, plans to go back on Victory Day, the anniversary of Bangladesh's triumph over Pakistan in the 1971 liberation war, her spokesperson said.

She was sentenced to death after being convicted of crimes against humanity for her role in the crackdown, in a trial held in her absence that raised questions about due process. Her Awami League party is banned in Bangladesh. The UN says as many as 1,400 people were killed by security forces during the uprising.

The government says she would be arrested immediately if she returned and has promised to carry out the death sentence.

Hasina now wants the Bangladesh government to arrange a flight from Delhi. If that fails, she could travel commercially or cross the land border.

"She is even prepared to walk into Bangladesh," Abu Obaidha Arin, a key aide to Hasina, told the BBC.

Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Sheikh Hasina fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule

India and Bangladesh share a 4,096km (2,545 mile) border across five Indian states - West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Her supporters, Arin said, had identified nine possible crossing points. "This is a carefully thought-out, precise plan. This is serious."

Dhaka has responded with defiance, insisting Hasina must be extradited.

"Reality and desire are different things," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs, told reporters in Dhaka. "[The reality is] she's not a regular commercial passenger. She can only be brought back in handcuffs."

India's foreign ministry said on Wednesday that Hasina's extradition request was being examined through the "established process", adding that a voluntary return would be a separate matter.

• Sheikh Hasina: The pro-democracy icon who became an autocrat

• Hasina's conviction for crimes against humanity is testing India-Bangladesh ties

Many in Dhaka believe Hasina's declaration is more than a promise of homecoming.

They believe it is an attempt to test the government's authority, force her way back into the political conversation and exploit divisions among the parties that united to oust her. It also threatens to turn India's unresolved problem of sheltering a former ally into a more immediate diplomatic crisis.

Over the past 18 months, he says, she has held more than 300 such meetings, reaching supporters across all 64 districts and the country's 300 constituencies. They are organised through the Awami League's 78 units and "can last four or five hours".

The meetings allow Hasina to listen directly to party workers, hear their grievances and understand what is happening on the ground, Arin says. He insists the response has been substantial and claims the party "could mobilise five million people to welcome her along the route from the border to Dhaka, forming a human chain".

"We have the organisational capacity to make that happen," he says.

That may be an ambitious claim. The Awami League remains a mass party with millions of supporters, but it is banned and largely shut out of mainstream politics. Much of its leadership is abroad, in jail or underground. Police have arrested supporters and filed thousands of cases against party workers.

Yet its supporters have continued to take to the streets, staging flash protests that have grown more frequent and confrontational in recent months.

Image caption,

Awami League supporters have staged flash protests across Bangladesh in recent months

Several districts have reported bomb attacks, arson and vandalism, though responsibility for some incidents remains disputed.

Gopalganj, Hasina's ancestral district, has proved particularly difficult for the authorities to control.

Awami League supporters have attacked police stations, external, torched vehicles and targeted homes and offices belonging to ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) leaders, reports say. Highways have been blocked, external with felled trees and burning tyres, bringing traffic to a standstill. In some areas, police have withdrawn, external amid fears of further attacks.

Supporters have staged 40 demonstrations and more than 140 riots up to 23 November, according to data from conflict monitoring group Acled (Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project). At least 11 people, including two civilians, have been killed in political violence this month, six directly linked to the unrest, the group says.

The party's ability to cause disruption, however, is not necessarily evidence of a broad resurgence.

Many in Dhaka remain sceptical that Hasina will actually return, viewing the announcement as a means of galvanising a demoralised party.

Yet the Awami League has achieved something politically: it is back in the conversation. Immediately after Hasina's fall, even mentioning the party was taboo. Now its future is being debated across the political spectrum.

Shafiqul Alam, editor of the English-language daily Daily Waadaa and former press secretary to the Muhammad Yunus-led interim government, believes the party is "exploiting cracks in the unity forged during the uprising".

He told the BBC that "disagreements" over the July Charter, external, proposed constitutional changes and the referendum have "widened divisions" between the elected BNP government and rivals Jamaat-e-Islami and the youth-led National Citizen Party (NCP).

Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Fire engulfs a police station in Gopalganj on 17 November amid unrest following the arrest of Awami League activists

"The Awami League sees an opening," Alam told the BBC. "The party believes this is an opportune moment to take to the streets, exploiting a weakened police force and divisions among the forces of the July uprising."

Analysts say if Hasina returns it could just as easily deepen hostility as revive her party's fortunes. The government has framed the sporadic recent violence as terrorism, while supporters insist their demonstrations are peaceful and accuse the authorities of repression.

The larger question is whether Bangladesh can sustain the exclusion of a political constituency as substantial as the Awami League without creating another source of instability.

For India, the dilemma is increasingly difficult to manage.

Delhi has sheltered Hasina, but her public remarks have angered Dhaka, which wants her extradited. India has sought to repair ties through diplomatic outreach and talks on trade, border security and other bilateral issues, but relations remain strained.

The chill is striking: nearly 10 months into his tenure, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has yet to visit India.

Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images

Image caption,

NCP members stage a motorcycle rally in Dhaka on 24 November, protesting against violence allegedly carried out by the banned Awami League

A trip was reportedly in the offing in August, but Hasina's press conference in Delhi proved a setback to efforts to reset relations.

Delhi, he says, "feels it has tried its best" to work with Rahman's government over the past 10 months - "from appointing a political heavyweight as high commissioner, external with cabinet rank to offering fresh talks on security and trade".

"The failure of this outreach has left India disillusioned with Dhaka. India seems to have decided that bilateral relations will likely remain tense whatever it does, so there is little reason to stop Hasina from stirring the political pot."

Delhi has the leverage to restrain Hasina from making political statements on Indian soil, Paliwal argues, but may not want to exercise it.

Nor, in his view, is it in India's interest to see the Awami League permanently excluded from Bangladeshi politics.

Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images

Image caption,

Bangladesh security forces patrol and conduct drills in Dhaka's Shahbagh area on the Awami League's founding anniversary

"The political party still enjoys pockets of support across Bangladesh and is weaved into the social and political fabric of the country," he says. "So, yes, it is in India's interest, and also in Bangladesh's long-term interests, to rehabilitate the Awami League and take the path of political reconciliation."

That view is increasingly contested in Dhaka.

"There is a perception in Bangladesh that India wants to rehabilitate the Awami League. There are issues India has not resolved, including the extradition of Hasina. India has also not renewed the transit facilities that could benefit Bangladeshi garment exporters, while the Ganges water treaty, external is nearing expiry without much progress. But has India done enough to win back trust?" says Alam.

"For now, only tourist and medical visas have resumed. Everything else remains in limbo."

A Dhaka-based foreign-policy expert, who asked not to be named, says the two countries remain locked in "mutual frustration".

Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

Vehicles pass a mural of Sheikh Hasina near Dhaka University

Hasina, he says, remains central to the impasse. "She remains the elephant in the room, but we also have to find a way to move beyond Hasina."

Paliwal argues that the least damaging outcome for India would be Hasina returning to face a fresh trial, with the Awami League rehabilitated under a different operational leadership.

"It will reintroduce a degree of balance in Bangladeshi politics, and will afford India space to protect its long-term interests and equities better," he says.

For now, 16 December is not yet a confirmed journey. But Hasina has already succeeded in making her return a question that neither Dhaka nor Delhi can ignore.

"December could be chaotic. Everyone in Dhaka is on edge," says the foreign-policy expert, warning of protests and confrontation as Hasina's proposed return date approaches - and the possibility that it could be postponed yet again.

"Hasina is unlikely to return, as she would face a death sentence. But her comments have clearly galvanized her supporters," says Pearl Pandya, Acled's South Asia analyst.

But the impasse is also complicating India's ties with Bangladesh. As Paliwal puts it, the "next window of serious negotiations will now open only after Hasina returns to Dhaka, or Dhaka relents under pressure and returns to the table".

My dad's watch stopped the moment he died - I found it in the ashes of Hong Kong tower fire

Mr So's parents, both in their 80s, were among the 168 people killed in last year's Hong Kong tower-block blaze - the deadliest the city had seen in decades.

Their building was the first of the Wang Fuk Court complex to catch fire, and their bodies were burned beyond recognition.

In this video Mr So, who is only using his surname, visits his parents' grave and shows what is left of his parents' possessions.

Zelensky questions 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview

Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced his frustration with the United States and questioned Donald Trump's relationship with Vladimir Putin in an interview with the BBC.

In a picture posted to Truth Social on Saturday, where Trump and Putin embrace, the US president described his Russian counterpart as "my friend".

"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky told the BBC's Sarah Rainsford at his office in central Kyiv.

"He [Putin] is an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be."

FAST

PARIS: Film star Gerard Depardieu, one of the leading faces of French cinema, will face trial on charges of raping actress Charlotte Arnould in 2018, after a Paris appeal court on Thursday (Nov 26) rejected his bid to avoid having the case tried.

NEW YORK: A powerful storm disrupted the Thanksgiving holiday along much of the US East Coast on Thursday (Nov 26), knocking out power for hundreds of thousands of users as wind gusts of up to 70 mph (112 kph) toppled trees and power lines.

Heavy rains flooded coastal areas, while utilities warned that rain-soaked ground and strong winds could increase the risk of falling trees and power outages.

Nearly 200,000 homes and businesses had no power in Virginia and another 177,000 in Maryland as of 2:26pm ET (Friday, 3.26am, Singapore time) according to poweroutage.us, which also showed Pennsylvania, New Jersey and North Carolina each had tens of thousands of utility customers without electricity.

items.title: Albania's youth are protesting, no longer leaving the country
items.summary: Youth protests against a rigid political system and corruption have shaken the government of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama. They also show that fewer young people are willing to emigrate in search of a better future.
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5PxaV

Most of the 'Flamingo Revolution' protests in Albania have been peaceful Image: Vlasov Sulaj/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Advertisement

In mid-October, students in the Albanian capital Tirana set a suitcase on fire and threw it into the courtyard of the Education Ministry. Everyone in the country understood the symbolism: According to the 2023 census, the population of this Western Balkan country shrunk by about 420,000 between 2011 and 2023 — by nearly 15% — primarily because of emigration.

For a generation of young Albanians, this was the response to a system that gave them little voice. But now young people want to stay, and the protesters are saying that the system has to change.

Known as the "Flamingo Revolution," the social movement began in May with demonstrations against a luxury resort in a coastal reserve that US President Donald Trump's daughter Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner were involved in.

It quickly evolved into broader criticism against corruption, Prime Minister Edi Rama's government and his ruling Socialist Party and the country's entire political class.

Thousands marched almost every evening for four months in protests that were largely peaceful. But on October 13, a student protest escalated and there were clashes with police. Since then, the unrest has continued, with police using tear gas, water cannons and rubber bullets against demonstrators. There have been hundreds of arrests and many injuries, amid damage to public and private property.

'Flamingo revolution' has broad support

The protesters have called for Rama's resignation, a transitional government, electoral reform and fresh elections. The movement, which has no leader, has support from people across the political spectrum. And while the prime minister has blamed "foreign hands" for the movement, there seems to be little evidence that external actors are orchestrating the protests, though they may have attempted to exploit the unrest online.

The protesters, who do not feel represented by Albania's democracy, are driven by domestic issues: corruption, the high cost of living and low wages. This is nothing new, but many factors have converged recently: a series of high-level corruption charges, including against ministers and two of Rama's former deputies, rising prices and the fact that Albania is being measured against EU standards by a new generation.

In certain areas, Rama has transformed Albania since taking office in 2013: the economy has grown significantly, as the government likes to point out, and tourism is booming. But the prosperity remains unevenly distributed. Critics accuse the government of channeling too much taxpayer money into a small number of well-connected companies through prestigious projects and public-private partnerships, and in some cases through corrupt business deals, at the expense of healthcare, education and better economic prospects for the wider population.

Rama has rejected the calls for his resignation and has invited protesters to engage in dialogue, which they have so far refused.

Clashes with police erupted in mid-October like here in TiranaImage: Adnan Beci/AFP

Alternating between Socialist and Democratic Party

In 2008, Rama and Sali Berisha, the long-time chairman of the opposition Democratic Party, worked on a reform to Albania's constitution and electoral law, which was approved by parliament. Since then, it is party leaders who have determined who enters Parliament, which weakens ties between lawmakers and their constituents.

In addition, it has become significantly more difficult for new parties to win seats. In 2025, a new party received about 64,000 votes, but only one seat. The Socialists, by contrast, won about one seat for every 10,000 votes.

Rama has been the leader of the Socialists since 2005, while Berisha first became the chairman of the Democratic Party in 1991. For 21 years, Albania's prime minister has either been Rama or Berisha. Freedom House, a US nongovernmental organization that promotes democracy worldwide, classifies Albania as "partly free" and describes the country's political parties as being "often organized around leading personalities."

Protesters on the streets have said that they want both men to be jailed. Rama has argued that governments should be replaced at the ballot box, not on the streets.

Though the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) acknowledged that parliamentary elections in 2025 were "competitive and professionally managed" it said that they had taken place "in a highly polarized environment and contestants did not enjoy a level playing field."

It added that there were "reports of intimidation, misuse of public resources and pressure on public employees, which undermined equal opportunities."

The Democratic Party also spoke of election fraud and intimidation. Turnout was below 45%.

Protesters call out corruption, face high cost of living

Many protesters also allege that when it comes to business, what matters is the proximity to people in power. They criticize the public procurement, public auctions and concessions system, which has led to state-owned land, including coastal and protected areas, being sold to private investors.

Ordinary Albanians are feeling the financial brunt. According to the Albanian Institute of Statistics (INSTAT), half of all employees earn less than 60,000 lek (roughly €620 or $680) per month after taxes. But according to Eurostat, food prices are slightly above the EU average and real estate prices in Tirana have nearly doubled since 2018, with rents rising just as quickly.

For many years, young Albanians who were dissatisfied with the system opted to leave the country. The number of Albanian citizens in Germany more than doubled between 2018 and 2024, reaching almost 120,000.

Though it is still too early to say whether there are fewer Albanians leaving today, for many protesters staying has become a political statement.

Albanians continue to call for the prime minister's resignationImage: Florion Goga/REUTERS

Albanians largely pro-EU

Rama has argued that his resignation would jeopardize Albania's bid to join the European Union by 2030, but the vast majority of Albanians are pro-European, including those on the streets and in the opposition. From the protesters' perspective, it is the government headed by Rama that is the real obstacle on the path to the EU.

Though there is currently a wave of protests across Europe, the only obvious comparison is with Serbia, where a student-led movement recently forced a long-time ruler from office. Whether Albania will follow this example depends on whether young people, who have traditionally not been deeply engaged in politics, can turn their protests into votes.

What is certain is that for three decades, Albania's leaders have relied on their citizens' suitcases. Now, the country's students have burned that very luggage.

Andi Balla is a doctoral candidate at the Leibniz Institute for East and Southeast European Studies (IOS) in Regensburg, where he is conducting research on demographic debates in Albania. He has written numerous articles on Albania for an international audience.

在谷歌上首选德国之声

阿尔巴尼亚大多数“火烈鸟革命”抗议活动都是和平的 图片：Vlasov Sulaj/NurPhoto/picture alliance

广告

10月中旬，阿尔巴尼亚首都地拉那的学生点燃了一个手提箱，并将其扔进教育部庭院。全国上下都明白这一象征意义：根据2023年人口普查，这个西巴尔干国家的人口在2011年至2023年间减少了约42万——近15%——主要原因是移民。

对一代阿尔巴尼亚年轻人来说，这是对一个几乎不给他们发言权的体制的回应。但现在年轻人想留下来，抗议者表示体制必须改变。

这场被称为“火烈鸟革命”的社会运动始于5月，当时示威活动反对一座位于海岸保护区的豪华度假村，美国总统唐纳德·特朗普的女儿伊万卡·特朗普及其丈夫贾里德·库什纳参与其中。

它很快演变为对腐败、总理埃迪·拉马政府及其执政的社会党以及该国整个政治阶层的更广泛批评。

四个月来，数千人几乎每晚都举行游行，抗议活动基本和平。但10月13日，一场学生抗议升级，与警察发生冲突。此后，骚乱持续不断，警察对示威者使用催泪瓦斯、水炮和橡皮子弹。已有数百人被捕，多人受伤，公共和私人财产遭到破坏。

“火烈鸟革命”获得广泛支持

抗议者呼吁拉马辞职、组建过渡政府、进行选举改革并举行新的选举。这场没有领导人的运动得到了各政治派别人士的支持。尽管总理将这场运动归咎于“外国之手”，但似乎几乎没有证据表明有外部行为者在策划抗议，不过他们可能试图在网上利用骚乱。

抗议者感到阿尔巴尼亚的民主没有代表他们，他们被国内问题所驱动：腐败、高昂的生活成本和低工资。这并非新鲜事，但许多因素最近汇聚在一起：一系列高层腐败指控，包括针对部长和拉马的两名前副手的指控，物价上涨，以及新一代人正以欧盟标准来衡量阿尔巴尼亚。

在某些领域，拉马自2013年上任以来改变了阿尔巴尼亚：经济显著增长，政府喜欢指出这一点，旅游业蓬勃发展。但繁荣仍然分配不均。批评者指责政府通过声望项目和公私合作伙伴关系，在某些情况下通过腐败的商业交易，将过多纳税人的钱输送给少数关系密切的公司，牺牲了医疗、教育和更广泛民众更好的经济前景。

拉马拒绝了辞职的呼吁，并邀请抗议者进行对话，但迄今为止他们拒绝了。

10月中旬在地拉那等地爆发了与警察的冲突 图片：Adnan Beci/AFP

在社会党与民主党之间交替

2008年，拉马和反对党民主党长期主席萨利·贝里沙共同推动了一项对阿尔巴尼亚宪法和选举法的改革，并获得议会批准。此后，由政党领导人决定谁进入议会，这削弱了议员与其选民之间的联系。

此外，新政党赢得席位的难度显著增加。2025年，一个新政党获得约6.4万张选票，但只赢得一个席位。相比之下，社会党大约每1万张选票赢得一个席位。

拉马自2005年以来一直是社会党领导人，而贝里沙于1991年首次成为民主党主席。21年来，阿尔巴尼亚的总理不是拉马就是贝里沙。自由之家，一个在全球推广民主的美国非政府组织，将阿尔巴尼亚列为“部分自由”，并称该国的政党“往往围绕主要人物组织”。

街头抗议者表示，他们希望两人都被监禁。拉马则主张政府应在投票箱而非街头被替换。

尽管欧洲安全与合作组织（OSCE）承认2025年的议会选举“具有竞争性且管理专业”，但表示选举发生在“高度两极化的环境中，竞争者没有享有公平的竞争环境”。

它还补充说，“有报道称存在恐吓、滥用公共资源和对公职人员的施压，这破坏了平等机会。”

民主党也谈到了选举舞弊和恐吓。投票率低于45%。

抗议者揭露腐败，面临高昂生活成本

许多抗议者还声称，在商业方面，重要的是与掌权者的关系。他们批评公共采购、公开拍卖和特许权制度，这导致国有土地，包括沿海和保护区的土地，被出售给私人投资者。

普通阿尔巴尼亚人正感受到经济压力。根据阿尔巴尼亚统计研究所（INSTAT）的数据，一半雇员的税后月收入低于6万列克（约620欧元或680美元）。但根据欧盟统计局的数据，食品价格略高于欧盟平均水平，地拉那的房地产价格自2018年以来几乎翻了一番，租金上涨速度同样快。

多年来，对体制不满的年轻阿尔巴尼亚人选择离开该国。2018年至2024年间，在德国的阿尔巴尼亚公民人数增加了一倍多，达到近12万人。

尽管现在说离开的阿尔巴尼亚人是否减少还为时过早，但对许多抗议者来说，留下来已成为一种政治表态。

阿尔巴尼亚人继续呼吁总理辞职 图片：Florion Goga/REUTERS

阿尔巴尼亚人总体上支持加入欧盟

拉马主张，他的辞职将危及阿尔巴尼亚到2030年加入欧盟的努力，但绝大多数阿尔巴尼亚人支持欧洲，包括街头抗议者和反对派。从抗议者的角度来看，拉马领导的政府才是通往欧盟道路上的真正障碍。

尽管目前欧洲各地出现抗议浪潮，但唯一明显的比较是塞尔维亚，那里一场由学生领导的运动最近迫使一位长期统治者下台。阿尔巴尼亚是否会效仿这一榜样，取决于传统上并未深度参与政治的年轻人能否将抗议转化为选票。

可以肯定的是，三十年来，阿尔巴尼亚的领导人一直依赖其公民的手提箱。现在，该国的学生烧毁了那件行李。

安迪·巴拉是雷根斯堡莱布尼茨东欧和东南欧研究研究所（IOS）的博士候选人，他在那里研究阿尔巴尼亚的人口辩论。他为国际读者撰写了大量关于阿尔巴尼亚的文章。

items.summary: The tanker carried up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel, but authorities reported no major spill and activated Spain’s Level 2 maritime pollution response plan.

Crew member dies after diesel tanker capsizes off Ibiza, no pollution so far

The tanker carried up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel, but authorities reported no major spill and activated Spain’s Level 2 maritime pollution response plan.

A rescue vessel moves next to the capsized oil tanker Med Emre off Ibiza, Spain, Nov 26, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/CGT Mar y Puertos)

MADRID: At least one crew member aboard a ship carrying diesel has died after the vessel capsized and partially sank off the Spanish island of Ibiza on Thursday (Nov 26), regional authorities said, adding there were no signs of pollution so far.

The Malta-flagged chemical tanker Med Emre was sailing from Algeciras to Barcelona and may have been carrying up to 7,000 metric tons of diesel when it keeled over about 30 nautical miles (56 km) off Ibiza's northwestern coast, the Balearic Islands' interior department said.

Emergency services said all 17 crew members were rescued, but one died after being taken directly to Ibiza's Can Misses hospital. Six others were brought to Ibiza airport and taken to two hospitals with light injuries, primarily hypothermia.

Of the remaining crew, five were taken to Valencia and five remained in good condition aboard a rescue vessel, they added.

Pablo Garriz, the Balearic Islands' regional head of emergencies, said the crew included Turkish and Indian nationals, but he could not yet confirm the nationality of the deceased.

The tanker remained partially submerged with its keel protruding above the surface, Garriz told reporters, despite initial indications that it had sunk completely.

"The positive news is that the vessel is not on the seabed but remains semi-submerged at the surface, which allows salvage and containment operations," he said, adding there was currently no impact on Balearic waters or coastline and no evidence of a significant spill, although small sheens had been observed.

Technical experts were assessing the vessel's stability before deciding on salvage and cargo-recovery operations, he added.

Spain's maritime rescue service sent an aircraft and a vessel specialised in oil-spill response, the Clara Campoamor, to survey the area. Three helicopters took part in the rescue, along with nearby merchant vessels.

Spain's merchant marine authority activated the national maritime pollution contingency plan at level 2, the second-highest.

The waters surrounding Ibiza are a habitat for sea turtles, dolphins and the Balearic shearwater, one of Europe's most threatened seabirds. The area is also home to extensive meadows of Posidonia oceanica seagrass, which plays a vital role in supporting marine biodiversity.

Spain's worst maritime environmental disaster occurred in 2002, when the Bahamas-flagged tanker Prestige sank off the northwestern Galicia region, spilling tens of thousands of tons of heavy fuel oil and fouling hundreds of beaches in Spain and France.

The Balearic regional government said it was gathering information on the accident and its possible consequences, including any risk of fuel pollution, before deciding on further measures.

RIYADH: The Saudi-led military coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said on Thursday (Nov 26) that the Iran-aligned group had attacked Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery, a day after hitting the largest oil refinery in the kingdom.

The refinery in the southwestern city of Jazan, near the Yemeni border, is designed to process up to 400,000 barrels of crude oil per day.

The coalition said it had later destroyed a ballistic missile launch platform in the Yemeni port city of Hodeidah, which it said the Houthis had used in Thursday's attack on the refinery.

Earlier it said that targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure would be met with a firm military response.

On Wednesday the Houthis claimed attacks on Ras Tanura, Saudi Arabia's largest refinery and a major crude export hub, and the Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan.

The Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted four drones over Ras Tanura and air defences had destroyed a drone near Jeddah Islamic Port.

The Houthis, who control the most populous areas of Yemen including the capital Sanaa, have launched missiles and drones at Saudi airports, oil facilities and office buildings since Yemen's civil war reignited in July, in a spillover from the US-Iran war.

The attacks have previously temporarily disrupted some of Aramco's operations and caused the cancellation of most international flights to Riyadh. They also forced Saudi Arabia to postpone or cancel major international events, including soccer's AFC Asian Cup and the flagship FII investment conference.

Fighting has intensified since the Houthis seized strategic territory along Yemen's Red Sea coast in September and advanced towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a vital shipping route for Gulf oil producers seeking access to the Red Sea.

items.title: Saudi pop music is thriving — but for the right reasons?
items.summary: As part of Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia's music scene has evolved hugely thanks to state funding and support. Local musicians and DJs are optimistic. But are they actually just helping prop up an authoritarian state?
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5Pp1R

Prefer DW on Google

Although there are no pictures of state figureheads at big Saudi events, attendees say they know the state funds festivals and they suspect plainclothes security staff monitor the crowd Image: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

Advertisement

Today, rapper Asayel Bishi is one of Saudi Arabia's rising hip-hop stars, signed to the country's biggest record label for new music, MDLBEAST. But not so long ago, she was making international headlines for a totally different reason.

In 2020, after Bishi released a music video for a song, "Bint Mecca," or "girl from Mecca," featuring people dancing in a local cafe, Mecca's governor called for the arrest of Bishi's whole production team. He said the video violated the holy city's local customs and traditions. In the end, the situation was resolved with a discussion about filming permits.

And by early 2023, Bishi was signed to MDLBEAST and has since racked up hundreds of thousands of streams on music platforms like Spotify.

In the past, other Saudi rappers have ended up in prison for similar, alleged transgressions. The fact that Bishi's story went a different way is probably partially because the 31-year-old's career path is on a similar trajectory to the Saudi pop music industry as a whole.

Music part of Vision 2030

As part of Saudi ruler Mohammed bin Salman's Vision 2030 plan, announced in 2016 and which aims to move the country away from economic dependence on oil, the country has poured billions into the local music industry.

The pace of development increased in 2019 after the country held its first major festival, Soundstorm, an annual event that now draws major international acts and over 400,000 guests. MDLBEAST was created then, primarily as the festival organizer. Since then, it has also become a record label, radio station, distributor, promoter and talent incubator.

After decades of bans on concerts, the first officially sanctioned music gigs began to be held in 2017. Here, visitors arrive at the Soundstorm music festival in Banban in December 2025Image: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

A recent report for the Saudi Music Commission suggests the music sector could be worth $500 million (€455 million) by 2034. But it's difficult to figure out how well Saudi pop is really doing now because independent monitoring of the sector only began relatively recently.

Streaming platform Spotify reports that people listening to Saudi-made music inside Saudi Arabia increased by 195% between 2020 and 2024. However, the most-streamed artists inside the country are still international.

'Tied to the destiny of crown prince'

Although there was a mostly-hidden Saudi music scene before this recent boom, observers say the growth of the Saudi music sector is not organic.

It's all about building an industry from the top down, Amr Abdelrahim, a researcher at Sciences Po in Paris, reported in a 2024 study. "After 2016, young middle-class musicians and creative professionals, who had been careful to avoid drawing official attention to their countercultural activities suddenly became central to the ambitions of the state," he wrote.

The careers of young Saudi acts — like Bishi, for example — "became tied to the destiny of the crown prince," the researcher explained.

The Saudi royal family has long dispersed money from Saudi oil sales to their subjects, in order to ensure economic dependence and loyalty. But, Abdelrahim argued, "what is new about Saudi investments in culture under MBS is an unprecedented degree of centralization and the emergence of new clientelist networks around the country's de-facto ruler," using a common abbreviation for Crown Prince Mohammed.

Those involved "are inadvertently participating in the consolidation of the Saudi regime," he argued.

Observers have noted the level of control around musical events in Saudi Arabia, with one researcher saying she was unable to find video evidence of bad behavior later, even though many visitors had filmed itImage: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

Observers say a lot of the new music businesses are vague about their ties to the state. But it's clear they couldn't work without the state's financial support and approval.

items.title: Nine injured, three critically, after Bangkok oil refinery explosion
items.summary: Black smoke could be seen across Bangkok's skyline after the blast, as officials urged residents to leave the area.
items.body:
Figure caption,

Watch: Fire and smoke billows out of refinery owned by energy company Bangchak Corporation

ByAlex Kleiderman

Updated 48 minutes ago

Seven people have been injured - four of them critically - after an explosion at an oil refinery in Bangkok, local government officials have said.

A fire broke out after the blast at the Phra Khanong facility run by energy giant Bangchak Corporation in the east of Thailand's capital at around 14:45 (07:45 GMT).

The company said the fire was brought under control and put out within 30 minutes, adding that the cause of the incident was being investigated.

Black smoke could be seen across Bangkok's skyline after the blast, while officials told residents to leave the area.

Image source, AFP via Getty Images

A alert sent to mobile phones by Bangkok authorities confirmed the fire was under control, but urged people to avoid the location.

Eyewitnesses shared video clips on social media of flames and smoke rising above the refinery.

The city-run Erawan Emergency Medical Centre said it was treating four "red" cases and three "yellow" - less severe - cases.

Bangchak Corporation said it had shut down production at the site, which can process up to 120,000 barrels of oil a day. The company has a second refinery in Chonburi province, about 50 miles (80km) from Bangkok, handling a capacity of about 180,000 barrels daily.

An explosion occurred at the Bangkok refinery in July 2012, sparking a fire but no reported injuries.

items.title: Congo Ebola outbreak reaches 12,000 cases as some responders evacuate
items.summary: As the fast-moving outbreak continues to spread in eastern Congo, fighting between rebels and the army is disrupting efforts to contain the spread of the disease.
items.body:
World

Congo Ebola outbreak reaches 12,000 cases as some responders evacuate

November 26, 20268:47 AM ET

By

The Associated Press

Relatives and healthcare workers prepare to bury a victim of Ebola, in Beni, North Kivu province, Congo, Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026.

Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP

hide caption

Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP

BUNIA, Congo (AP) — The fast-moving Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo has topped 12,000 confirmed cases, government data showed Thursday, as fighting between rebels and the army disrupts efforts to contain the spread of the disease.

It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history and nearly half the 12,021 people confirmed to have the virus have died, according to data from Congo's Ministry of Health. It is also the deadliest of Congo's 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.

The outbreak declared in May is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Response teams are battling armed conflict, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation.

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of people who are sick or have died from the disease. Containing the disease requires quickly identifying and treating patients in isolation, monitoring people who may have been exposed and safely burying the dead.

Fighting between the army and the Convention pour la révolution populaire rebels resumed Thursday morning in Iga-Barrière, a mining town about 25 kilometers (15 miles) north of Bunia in eastern Congo, sending new waves of displaced people toward the city. Bunia is the capital of northeastern Ituri province and a major hub for the Ebola response.

CRP is one of more than 100 armed groups in eastern Congo, where conflict has created one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises. The group was founded last year by former warlord Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted by the International Criminal Court in 2012 of recruiting children under 15 and using them in fighting.

Fighting between the army and the rebels earlier this week had already prevented teams from reaching some communities, disrupted monitoring of people exposed to the virus and left some treatment centers with fewer staff, Dr. Catherine Smallwood, the World Health Organization's Ebola incident manager, said Wednesday.

Smallwood said that about a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia on Tuesday after three full days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.

items.title: North Korea's Kim vows to build more nuclear weapons after ignoring Trump's overture
items.summary: Leader Kim Jong Un reportedly visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons to cope with threats from the U.S. and South Korea.
items.body:
World

North Korea's Kim vows to build more nuclear weapons after ignoring Trump's overture

November 26, 20268:31 AM ET

By

The Associated Press

In this photo provided by the North Korean government, leader Kim Jong Un inspects a facility the government says is for producing weapons-grade nuclear material at an undisclosed location in North Korea, Monday, Nov. 25, 2026.

Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service via AP

hide caption

Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service via AP

SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons, days after ignoring U.S. President Donald Trump's offer to meet during his recent visit to Asia.

Experts say Kim likely wants to show off his evolving nuclear arsenal, the backbone of his authoritarian rule, and reaffirm his rejection of any future talks on dismantling his nuclear program.

The North's official Korean Central News Agency said Thursday that Kim inspected two nuclear materials production factories, one newly inaugurated and the other being expanded. KCNA photos showed Kim and senior military officials walking between dense rows of what appeared to be centrifuges used to produce weapons-grade uranium and touring halls displaying what were believed to be warheads. Some of the images were blurred.

KCNA said Kim visited a nuclear-powered equipment production base and a nuclear research institute as well on Wednesday.

North Korea has disclosed a uranium enrichment site a few times since it showed one at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex to visiting American scholars in 2010. North Korea didn't say where the nuclear materials production factories that Kim visited this week are located. In June, when North Korea disclosed parts of a uranium enrichment site while reporting on Kim's visit there, outside experts assessed it was likely an additional uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon.

Kim justifies nuke program by citing threats from US, South KoreaKim said his latest inspection visit was part of efforts to strengthen North Korea's defense capabilities in response to "variable nuclear threats approaching the Korean Peninsula moment by moment." He accused the U.S. of inciting its regional allies to possess nuclear-powered submarines and committing to sharing its nuclear weapons with them, KCNA said.

"The validity and substantiality of our possession of nuclear weapons and the trend of bolstering up its nuclear capability in quality and quantity are an irreversible reality," Kim said, according to KCNA.

Kim also said the deployment of low-yield battlefield nuclear weapons across multiple domains for various missions is crucial and urgent given North Korea's "inevitable reality facing the border with the most dangerous enemy state," a reference to South Korea. North Korea has in recent years focused on developing such tactical nuclear weapons amid heightened animosity with South Korea.

"Trump has talked about a willingness to meet Kim Jong Un, but the basic U.S. position that North Korea must denuclearize remains unchanged. So Kim Jong Un wants to say 'Look at how powerful we are. Don't talk about denuclearization if you want to meet us,'" said Moon Seong Mook, an analyst for the Seoul-based Korea Research Institute for National Strategy.

Moon said Kim's visit to the nuclear facilities was also likely meant to check on how state objectives on the nuclear program have progressed this year and what future goals must be set ahead of a year-end Workers' Party conference.

South Korea's Defense Ministry said it takes Kim's comments on battlefield nuclear weapons seriously and added that Seoul maintains a firm military readiness against Pyongyang's nuclear threats under an alliance with the U.S. South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff declined to share an analysis of the North Korean nuclear facilities reported by KCNA, calling it confidential information for South Korea and the U.S.

Trump still hopes to meet KimTrump reiterated his eagerness to restore diplomacy with Kim as he visited China last week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. But a Trump-Kim meeting didn't happen, with Pyongyang not publicly responding to Trump's overture.

In an interview with the New York Post this week, Trump dismissed the suggestion that Kim had rebuffed his outreach, saying, "No, he didn't ignore it. You know, we had many leaders there … There'll be a time when we meet … It was just not really the right time. It was a very busy two-day period."

Trump also claimed he could revive diplomacy with Kim at any time by restarting the exchange of letters they maintained during his first term, although he acknowledged that the two leaders had not corresponded "recently."

Kim has previously said he could return to talks if the U.S. drops its "hostile policy" against his country and respects what he calls the North's status as a nuclear state. Experts say Kim aims to win international recognition as a nuclear state so that he could demand the lifting of international sanctions.

Last week, International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi assessed North Korea has been expanding its original uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon, calling the move "a cause for serious concern."

Nuclear weapons can be built using either highly enriched uranium or weapons-grade plutonium, and North Korea has facilities to produce both at Yongbyon. Last year, South Korea's Unification Minister Chung Dong-young said that North Korea was operating four uranium enrichment facilities and that they were running every day.

translation.body:
世界

朝鲜金正恩无视特朗普的会面提议后誓言建造更多核武器

2026年11月26日 上午8:31 东部时间

作者

美联社

在这张朝鲜政府提供的照片中，领导人金正恩于2026年11月25日星期一在朝鲜一处未公开地点视察政府所称用于生产武器级核材料的设施。

朝鲜中央通讯社/朝鲜新闻社 via 美联社

隐藏图注

朝鲜中央通讯社/朝鲜新闻社 via 美联社

韩国首尔（美联社）——朝鲜领导人金正恩视察了生产核原料的设施，并呼吁建造更多核武器。几天前，他无视了美国总统唐纳德·特朗普在最近访问亚洲期间提出的会面提议。

专家表示，金正恩很可能想展示其不断发展的核武库——这是他威权统治的支柱——并重申他拒绝未来就拆除其核计划进行任何谈判。

朝鲜官方媒体朝鲜中央通讯社周四表示，金正恩视察了两家核材料生产工厂，其中一家新近落成，另一家正在扩建。朝中社照片显示，金正恩和高级军事官员走在密集排列的、看似用于生产武器级铀的离心机之间，并参观了展示据信为弹头的展厅。部分图像被模糊处理。

朝中社称，金正恩周三还视察了一个核动力设备生产基地和一个核研究所。

自2010年向到访的美国学者展示其主要宁边核综合设施的一处铀浓缩设施以来，朝鲜已数次公开铀浓缩设施。朝鲜没有说明金正恩本周视察的核材料生产工厂位于何处。今年6月，朝鲜在报道金正恩视察时公开了一处铀浓缩设施的部分内容，外部专家评估那很可能是宁边的一处额外铀浓缩设施。

金正恩以美国和韩国的威胁为由为核计划辩护。金正恩表示，他最近的视察是其加强朝鲜防御能力努力的一部分，以应对“时刻逼近朝鲜半岛的变幻莫测的核威胁”。据朝中社报道，他指责美国煽动其地区盟友拥有核动力潜艇，并承诺与其分享核武器。

据朝中社报道，金正恩说：“我们拥有核武器的正当性和实质性，以及我们在质量和数量上加强核能力的趋势，是不可逆转的现实。”

金正恩还表示，鉴于朝鲜“面临与最危险敌对国家接壤的不可避免的现实”——指的是韩国——在多个领域部署用于各种任务的低当量战场核武器至关重要且紧迫。近年来，随着与韩国敌意加剧，朝鲜一直专注于发展此类战术核武器。

“特朗普谈到了愿意与金正恩会面，但美国要求朝鲜无核化的基本立场没有改变。所以金正恩想说‘看看我们有多强大。如果想见我们，就别谈无核化’，”首尔韩国国家战略研究院分析师文成默说。

文成默表示，金正恩视察核设施也可能意在检查国家核计划目标今年取得了哪些进展，以及在年底劳动党会议之前必须设定哪些未来目标。

韩国国防部表示，韩方严肃对待金正恩关于战场核武器的言论，并补充说，首尔在韩美同盟下对平壤的核威胁保持坚定的军事戒备。韩国联合参谋本部拒绝分享对朝中社报道的朝鲜核设施的分析，称这是韩国和美国的机密信息。

特朗普仍希望与金正恩会面。特朗普上周访问中国出席亚太经济合作组织峰会时重申了他恢复与金正恩外交的渴望。但特朗普与金正恩的会面并未发生，平壤没有公开回应特朗普的提议。

本周在接受《纽约邮报》采访时，特朗普驳斥了金正恩拒绝其示好的说法，称：“不，他没有无视。你知道，我们在那里有很多领导人……总会有我们见面的时候……只是当时时机不太合适。那是非常忙碌的两天。”

特朗普还声称，他随时可以通过重启他们在其第一个任期内保持的信件往来来恢复与金正恩的外交，尽管他承认两位领导人“最近”没有通信。

金正恩此前曾表示，如果美国放弃对朝鲜的“敌对政策”并尊重他所称的朝鲜核国家地位，他就可以重返谈判。专家表示，金正恩旨在赢得国际社会对其核国家地位的承认，以便要求解除国际制裁。

上周，国际原子能机构总干事拉斐尔·格罗西评估称，朝鲜一直在扩建其位于宁边的原有铀浓缩设施，称此举“令人严重关切”。

核武器可以用高浓缩铀或武器级钚制造，朝鲜在宁边拥有生产这两种材料的设施。去年，韩国统一部长官郑东泳表示，朝鲜运营着四个铀浓缩设施，且每天都在运行。
